name: Tirio
confidence_why: The only statement on Baramu (Tirio) stress is Wurm's 1971 family-level remark, from what he himself calls a superficial and tentative study, that stress "appears to be phonemic" across the Tirio family, and the one modern phonetic study of a Tirio-family language, Rogers 2021 on the sister language Bitur, found no contrastive stress at all, so the lexical-stress record rests on a single hedged remark that nothing confirms.

catalog_quote: The phonology of the languages of the Tirio Family is relatively complex. The results of a superficial phonological study are still tentative, but they seem to possess the following consonant phonemes: [...] The bracketed phonemes are doubtful. The vowel phonemes appear to be: a æ e i o u œ ə. Vowel length is phonemic. Several diphthongs occur. Stress appears to be phonemic, and a complex rhythm system is present. No tonal system has been observed. The syllable structure is comparatively simple and open syllables consisting of C+V or C+V+V are overwhelmingly predominant initially and medially.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Tirio (Lower Fly) family as a whole, including Tirio (=Baramu), Wurm tentatively reports contrastive (lexically unpredictable) word stress interacting with a 'complex rhythm system', phonemic vowel length, and no tone; no positional rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described beyond the mention of a 'complex rhythm system' (cf. Wurm 1975: 334 'complex stress system with rhythm principles' for the whole Trans-Fly Stock).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('appears to be', 'superficial.. tentative').
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level typological summary (Tirio=Baramu, Aturu, Lewada-Dewara, Mutum), not a Baramu-specific description; word-level presumably, no citation forms with stress marks given. For sister language Bitur (Wurm's Mutum) Rogers 2021 finds no contrastive stress (length-based non-contrastive prominence), so the claim should be treated as provisional for Baramu.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement is FAMILY-LEVEL: Wurm 1971 sec. 3.32.3 describes 'the languages of the Tirio Family' jointly = Tirio (language of Tirio village, ~280 speakers), Aturu, Lewada-Dewara and Mutum/Paswam. Wurm's/Ray's/Riley's 'Tirio' is the language of Tirio village, which is Baramu [bmz] (Glottolog hh annotation on Lean 1986: 'Tirio of Ray/Riley = Baramu [bmz]'; Usher, NewGuineaWorld 'Lower Fly River': 'Riley (1931-1932: 172-189) 415 comparative terms for Tirio (Baramu)'; Jore & Aleman 2002 took their Baramu list in village 'Tirio #2'); it is NOT the retired ISO 'Tirio' [tcr]/Makayam [aup]. Wurm's other members map to Makayam [aup] (Aturu, Lewada-Dewara) and Bitur [mcc] (Mutum). For the sister language Bitur, Rogers 2021 (instrumental) finds no contrastive stress, which weakens Wurm's tentative family-wide 'phonemic stress' claim as applied to Baramu.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened for Baramu itself, so there is no new conflict on the catalog item. The only tension is indirect: Wurm 1971 (family-level, self-described 'superficial.. tentative', p. 144, re-verified on the page render held by the project: 'Vowel length is phonemic. Several diphthongs occur. Stress appears to be phonemic, and a complex rhythm system is present. No tonal system has been observed.') asserts phonemic stress for the whole 'Tirio Family', whereas Rogers 2021 finds no contrastive stress in the sister language Bitur, only length-cued non-contrastive lexical stress. Both agree there is no tone. Since Rogers describes Bitur, not Baramu, this is not a contradiction of the Baramu record, but it flags Wurm's family-level 'phonemic stress' as unconfirmed for any individual Lower Fly language.

sources.citation: Rogers, Phillip G. 2021. The phonetics of Bitur. In Kate L. Lindsey & Dineke Schokkin (eds), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 24), 108-119. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10125/24996
sources.note: Sister language Bitur [mcc], not Baramu: sec.4 'There is no lexical tone or contrastive stress in Bitur. Vowel length is not contrastive, but it seems to be the most salient prosodic feature.. it is possible to analyze Bitur as having lexical (non-contrastive) stress of which the primary acoustic correlate is length.' Intro p.108: Lower Fly research 'limited to wordlists.. and a one-page typological description (Wurm 1971)'.
